The finale of one of these works by this composer begins with four bars of a second-inversion E diminished seventh chord, played in a dotted rhythm in 2/4 time. The first movement of that one of these pieces by this composer begins with descending and ascending unison arpeggios in F minor in 12/8 time and is marked Allegro assai. Another of these works by this composer begins with a long C-minor chord in a (*) Grave (GRAH-vay) tempo and has an A-flat major Adagio cantabile theme in its second movement. One that begins with C-sharp triplet arpeggios, in a movement marked Adagio sostenuto, was given its nickname by Ludwig Rellstab, who envisioned the title phenomenon over Lake Lucerne. For 10 points, name these works for solo piano that include the Appassionata, Pathetique, and Moonlight.
2.r: piano sonatas by Ludwig Van Beethoven [prompt on partial answers]

2.q: A Chicago bandleader who played this instrument used the theme song 'Rosetta', and is called the 'father' of this instrument in jazz. 'Pannonica' and 'Bemsha Swing' are songs by a player of this instrument, which was also played by Earl Hines. Songs like 'Tea for Two' were performed quickly in 'cutting (*) contests' for this instrument, players of which include the composer of 'Round Midnight' and Art Tatum. For 10 points, Count Basie and Thelonious Monk played which instrument with 88 keys?

This man collaborated with Sonny Rollins and Sonny Stitt on the album Sonny Side Up. Arturo Sandoval was primarily influenced by this musician, who replaced his idol Roy Eldridge in the Teddy Hill big band. This composer of the standard "Blue 'N Boogie" collaborated with Max Roach, Bud Powell, Charles Mingus, and Charlie Parker on the album (*) Jazz at Massey Hall. More famous standards composed by him include "Groovin' High," "Manteca," and "Salt Peanuts." Unusual aspects of his playing style included puffing out his cheeks to a massive size and playing an instrument whose bell was bent upward 45 degrees. For 10 points, name this jazz trumpeter famous for co-founding bebop with Charlie Parker.

Pauline Viardot came out of retirement to premiere a C minor piece by this composer for contralto solo, male chorus, and orchestra, written as a wedding gift for Julie Schumann. A piece by this composer introduces its motif of a rising major third followed by a rising half-step in its first lyrics, "selig sind ("ZAY-lick zint")." This composer of the Schicksalslied ("SHICKS-alz-leet") used the text of Goethe's Harzreise im Winter for his (*) Alto Rhapsody. This composer wrote Four Serious Songs after Clara Schumann suffered a stroke. The death of this composer's mother inspired a seven-movement choral work that this composer set to passages from the Luther Bible rather than traditional Latin liturgical text. For 10 points, name this composer of A German Requiem.

In a work by this composer, two timpanis playing sextuplets introduce a movement whose main melody begins with two octaves of a descending G minor scale. This composer included pieces named for Sardanapalus and Cleopatra in a set of cantatas that won him the Prix ("pree") de Rome after four tries. This composer included a version of the Rakoczi March in his choral work (*) The Damnation of Faust. A work by this composer that ends with an "Orgy of the Brigands" was commissioned by Paganini as a viola concerto. This composer's unrequited love for Harriet Smithson inspired a work whose opium-induced visions are linked by an idee fixe. For 10 points, name this composer of Harold in Italy and Symphonie fantastique.

A composer from this country who espoused "new lyricism" evoked flower petals in his piano concerto "Memo Flora." The Debussy-inspired Quotation of Dream is by a composer from this country who used the "S-E-A" motif. An orchestra accompanies this country's traditional instruments in November Steps, which was premiered by a conductor from this country who directed the Boston Symphony Orchestra for 29 years. The (*) pentatonic in and yo scales are used in music from this country, which often features a four-stringed lute played with a bachi plectrum. A composer from this country wrote "Merry-Go-Round of Life" for the film Howl's Moving Castle. For 10 points, name this country home to Joe Hisaishi and Toru Takemitsu.

Most complex time signatures in Arabic music are found in a genre for this instrument called Muwashshah which spread from al-Andalus. This instrument attempts to mimic the sound of bagpipes in the Scottish musical form Puirt a beul ("Purscht ah beal"). Overtones create the effect of multiple lines in the Khoomei style for this instrument, which originates in the region of (*) Tuva. In Western classical music, the vibrato technique originated with this instrument. Twentieth century music for this instrument often incorporates its semi-pitchless technique of sprechgesang ("sprek-geh-sahng"). High notes can be produced using this instrument's falsetto register. For 10 points, name this instrument which is featured without accompaniment in a cappella ensembles.
2.r: human voice [accept singing or singers; accept specific voice ranges like soprano, alto, tenor, or bass; accept voice box or larynx; prompt on human or human body]

2.q: A motif referencing this non-Beethoven composer was incorporated into an Opus 28 string quartet that Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge commissioned from Anton Webern. This composer inspired a 25-movement Paul Hindemith piece whose "Postlodium" is the retrograde inversion of its "Praeludium," his Ludus Tonalis. Arnold Schoenberg used a tone row inspired by this composer in his Variations for Orchestra. A C major prelude by this earlier composer inspired a Dmitri Shostakovich cycle of solo (*) piano pieces in all major and minor keys. The third subject of this composer's incomplete Contrapunctus 14 begins with his namesake motif, a musical cryptogram of the notes [read slowly] "B-flat, A, C, B-natural." For 10 points, name this composer of The Art of Fugue and The Well-Tempered Clavier.
2.r: Johann Sebastian Bach [or J. S. Bach; accept BACH motif]

2.q: Much of this composer's earlier work was revived thanks to editions and advocacy by H. C. Robbins Landon. The introduction to this composer's last symphony opens with the orchestra in unison using a double-dotted rhythm to play the ascending fifth "D, D, D A." The second movement of one of his symphonies begins with the slow eighth notes "C C, E E, G G, E." Another symphony by this composer is unusually in F-sharp minor, ends with the musicians one by one (*) leaving the stage, and was written while in residence for Prince Esterhazy. For a 1791 trip, this composer wrote a symphony whose slow movement is interrupted by a sudden G-major chord. For 10 points, name this Classical composer whose 104 symphonies have nicknames like "Farewell," "London," and "Surprise."

This word, paired with "expression," describes a mechanism to control the volume of a pipe organ. This word's namesake "point" describes a held or repeated bass note against which dissonances are played. In organ music, this technique is used to play notes on the third staff. Usage of this technique can be dictated by the directives una corda and tre corde. In (*) piano music, this technique is notated by a long horizontal line under the grand staff, which may notch upwards to indicate that this technique should be "refreshed." The most common form of this mechanism lifts the dampers off of the piano strings, allowing them to vibrate freely and produce a resonating sound. For 10 points, name these foot-operated mechanisms on the bottom of a piano.
2.r: pedal [or pedal point; or foot pedal; or soft pedal; or sostenuto pedal; or sustain pedal; or damper pedal; prompt on using one’s feet]

2.q: The refrain of a bass aria in this opera begins with the melody [read slowly] "C [pause], D [pause], C, low A [pause], A". After fortune telling cards predict one character's death in this opera, she sings the "card" aria "En vain pour eviter". That character seduces another character by dancing a seguidilla ("SEG-uh-DEE-yah"). An aria in this opera ends with the title character throwing a (*) flower, and claims that "love is a rebellious bird". This opera's aria "Votre toast, je peux vous le rendre" ("voh-truh toast, je puh voo luh rawn-druh") is also called the "Toreador Song". The title character of this opera is killed by Don Jose ("don zhoh-SAY") in a fit of jealousy over the bullfighter Escamillo ("es-ca-mi-LLO"). For 10 points, name this Georges Bizet opera about a Spanish Roma woman.

A late piece this composer may have written for the opening of a casino contains a four-note motif taken from a setting of the Pange lingua found in Gradus ad Parnassum. One of this composer's symphonies begins with eighth, quarter, quarter, quarter, eighth rhythm played successively on [read slowly] G, D, E-flat and low F-sharp. A symphony by this composer begins with split viola accompaniment before the violins introduce a (*) short-short-long motif. The whole notes [read slowly] C, D, F, E start the last movement of one of this composer's symphonies which culminates in a five-voice fugato. This composer's only two minor-key symphonies are the "Little" and "Great" G minor. For 10 points, name this Classical composer of the "Jupiter" symphony.
2.r: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart [or Johannes Chrysostomus Wolfgangus Theophilus Mozart]

2.q: In a piece by a composer from this country, eight voices recite the first page of Beckett's The Unnameable and pay homage to Martin Luther King Jr. in the movement "O King." A composer from this country set farewell letters written by resistance fighters on the eves of their executions by the Nazis in a work whose title translates to "The Suspended Song." The former composer from this country is best known for his fourteen Sequenza. Another composer from this country depicted his visit to a snake research facility in his (*) Brazilian Impressions and composed three suites based on Renaissance lute pieces. That composer from here incorporated a phonograph recording of a nightingale in the second entry of a "trilogy" that also depicts the "festivals" and "fountains" of this country's capital. For 10 points, name this country, home to Luigi Nono, Luciano Berio, and Ottorino Respighi.

Margaret Leng Tan is best known for playing a type of this instrument. Each piece in a collection for this instrument uses a different unit size for its complex, nested, "square root form" proportions and illustrates a different emotion, like heroism or eroticism, from Indian aesthetics. A soprano vocalise is amplified by one of them in Ancient Voices of Children by George Crumb. Space constraints for a performance of Syvilla Fort's ballet Bacchanale inspired the (*) first true use of a type of this instrument. This instrument's extended techniques are used in Aeolian Harp, The Banshee, and The Tides of Manaunaun by Henry Cowell. Sonatas and Interludes was composed for a type of this instrument in which objects like screws, bolts, and rubber are placed on its strings, its "prepared" type. For 10 points, what instrument does the performer of John Cage's 4'33" sit in front of silently?

In his Harmonie universelle, Marin Mersenne wrote about "transcribing the riches and beauties" of this instrument onto the grand staff. In 1652, the death of a player of this instrument named Blancrocher led to the composition of two tombeaux for this instrument by Denis Gaultier and Francois Dufaut. A technique for playing this instrument consisted of playing a line of notes on alternating courses, a type of irregular arpeggiation known as style brise. Hundreds of songs for this instrument were written by English composer (*) John Dowland. It's not cello or harpsichord, but a suite for this instrument written by J. S. Bach contains an oft-performed Bourree in E minor. For 10 points, name this plucked string instrument that typically has a short neck and a rounded back, popular during the Renaissance era.

This instrument plays a lively duet with the snare drum in the "Ballerina's Dance" of Stravinsky's 1946 revision of Petrushka. A solo for this instrument appears in the second movement of Vaughan Williams's A Pastoral Symphony, where the musician is instructed to imitate this instrument's "natural type". The Sanctus hymn is played by an offstage one of these instruments in the second movement of Respighi's (*) Pines of Rome. A "felt crown" mute is used on this instrument during its laidback solo in Gershwin's An American in Paris. This instrument repeats a short-short-short-long rhythm on C# to open the funeral march beginning of Mahler's Symphony No. 5. For 10 points, name this high pitched brass instrument with three valves.

Leos Janacek ("LAY-osh YA-na-check") wrote a piece in this genre inspired by his relationship with Kamila Stosslova. Felix Mendelssohn's sixth and final work in this genre was written as a homage to hissister Fanny, who had died earlier that year. A pentatonic F major melody opens Antonin Dvorak's twelfth work in the genre, which is subtitled (*) American. Schubert took the theme for the second movement of a D minor work in this genre from one of his earlier songs, "Death and the Maiden." It's not a symphony, but Haydn was called the 'father' of this genre, having written 68 examples. For 10 points, name this genre of chamber music for cello, viola and two violins.

Queen recorded a cover version of this song for the film Highlander that plays from a car radio during the movie. A famous cover version of this song changes the lyric "come on, come through" from the original to "It's up to you." One of this song's writers Frank Ebb later declared that he "didn't even like" the repeated use of the phrase (*) "A-number-one" in a cover version of this song. This song is played immediately after "Auld Lang Syne" during New Years' celebrations in Times Square. Yankee Stadium was asked by Liza Minelli to stop playing the original version of this song after lost games. Originally recorded for a 1977 Martin Scorsese film, for 10 points name this song about the most populous city in the United States that was famously covered by Frank Sinatra.
2.r: Theme From New York, New York (or just New York, New York)

2.q: Johann Pachelbel's works in this genre are unique in that they feature no sections of imitative counterpoint, and consistently use long pedal points. It's not a partita, but meditative affetti sections alternates with fast-running passaggi sections in Girolami Frescobaldi's two books of pieces in this genre. This genre titles the final movements of Widor's fifth organ symphony and Ravel's Le (*) Tombeau de Couperin. A long mordent on A followed by a descending D minor scale opens one organ piece in this genre. Popular in the Baroque era, this fast-moving type of work for showing off virtuosity came from the Italian word for "touch." For 10 points, name this genre paired with a fugue in a famous D minor work by J.S. Bach.

The New York State Theatre's opening ceremony featured an antiphonal performance of an Igor Stravinsky piece in this genre. In 1942, the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra premiered 18 pieces in this genre commissioned by Eugene Goosens, including one "for American Heroes" by William Grant Still. Conductor Marin Alsop is the dedicatee of a piece in this genre by Joan Tower, whose title alludes to an earlier piece in this genre which opens with timpani, bass drum, and tam-tam, followed by (*) trumpets playing the ascending notes F, B-flat, F. Leo Arnaud's "Bugler's Dream" is in this genre and is used for television presentations of the Olympic Games. Elongated horns designed to hang banners name, for 10 points, pieces in what genre, one of which Aaron Copland wrote "for the Common Man"?
2.r: fanfares [accept fanfarade; accept flourish; accept Fanfare for American Heroes; accept Fanfare for a New Theatre; accept Fanfare for the Uncommon Woman; accept Fanfare for the Common Man]

2.q: This composer borrowed from the Te Deum of Antonio Urio for a succession of three fugues in "O fatal Consequences of Rage" from his work describing the life of Saul. An Allegro movement by this composer begins with the soprano singing long D, down to short A-B-A, then a repeat of that same motif. A work by this composer was controversial until a 1750 performance at the Foundling Hospital. This composer's set of four (*) anthems includes Zadok the Priest, which has been performed at all English coronations since that of George II. A work by this composer contains the sections "All We like Sheep" and "For Unto Us a Child is Born". The "Hallelujah Chorus" appears in, for 10 points, what composer's oratorio Messiah?
2.c: 2019 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt J. Packet 10 Q8

2.q: A bandleader who plays this instrument had a video installation at the 2017 Whitney Biennial which used his piece "Truth" from his album Harmony of Difference. That bandleader who plays this instrument composed the tracks "Changing of the Guard" and "The Rhythm Changes" for his three hour album The Epic. Kamasi Washington plays this instrument, as does a hard bop musician known for albums like The Bridge and one called this instrument Colossus. That man is (*) Sonny Rollins. Another player of this instrument used a gong hit to open an album featuring movements called "Acknowledgment" and "Resolution." For 10 points, the albums A Love Supreme and My Favorite Things were made by John Coltrane, a player of what instrument?
2.r: tenor saxophone [accept alto or baritone or soprano saxophone]
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt E. Packet 5 Q10

2.q: This work's third movement, in 12/8 time, is marked "Larga alla Siciliana," indicating it should be played like a Pifa dance. The public rehearsal of this work at the Vauxhall Gardens caused a major traffic disruption. This work, which opens with a French overture, alludes to the occasion of its commission with sections titled "Peace" and "Rejoicing", or "La Paix" and "La (*) Rejouissance". At its premiere, the collapse of a bas relief of George II caused a Servandoni-designed building to catch fire. This work was composed to commemorate the 1748 signing of the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle. For 10 points, name this wind band suite by George Frideric Handel meant to accompany a celebratory pyrotechnic display.
2.r: Music for the Royal Fireworks [accept anything mentioning Royal Fireworks]
2.c: 2013 Minnesota Undergraduate Tournament (MUT) Pkt HPacket 8 Proofread Q3

2.q: This language's term for "subtler art" names a Mannerism-era musical style. Five choirs of eight voices each are used in a choral work in this language by Thomas Tallis. This language's term for "fixed song" describes melodies such as "the armed man", which was itself used by Josquin des Prez (zhos-kan day pray) for two works in this language. The most famous work by Hildegard of Bingen is a (*) morality play written in this language. An apocryphal story about how Palestrina "saved" polyphony involves a work that sets text in this language, the Pope Marcellus Mass. For 10 points, name this language used in Roman Catholic services in the Renaissance, which was also used to write pieces titled Spem in alium and Ordo virtutum.

One of these instruments called a doira is commonly found in shashmaqam ensembles. A technique for playing these instruments called "tek" is used for playing Beledi and Maqsoum music in Egypt. Syahi paste is applied to tune one of these instruments from the Indian subcontinent which produces syllables known as bols, and which consists of a dayan and bayan. One of these instruments which is commonly called a (*) doumbek or darbouka commonly provides accompaniment to belly dance music. These instruments are often hourglass-shaped in North and West Africa, including a skin-covered "goblet" variant called the djembe, which skilled performers are said to make "talk". The tabla is an example of, for 10 points, what percussion instruments that include a "snare" variety?
2.r: drums [accept goblet drums; accept djembe or tabla before either is read; prompt on percussion]

2.q: An orchestra in this city recorded Beethoven's fifth symphony on the Voyager Golden Record. A conductorless Baroque orchestra founded in a church in this city recorded the soundtrack to Amadeus. Andre Previn simultaneously served as principal conductor for two orchestras in this city, where he hosted his "Music Night" television program. After Walter Legge suspended an orchestra he founded in this city, that ensemble collectivized into a "new" version under conductor Otto Klemperer, who spent much of his later career in this city. The (*) Philharmonia orchestra is based in this city, where Neville Mariner founded the Academy of St Martin in the Fields. In this city, Henry Wood started a series of summer concerts whose popular "Last Night" traditionally includes the first Pomp & Circumstance march. For 10 points, name this city where the Proms are held annually in Royal Albert Hall.

In one performance of this opera, Antonello Palombi was thrown on stage in street clothes to replace Roberto Alagna after he was booed by the audience. This opera's premiere was delayed due to scenery and costumes being stuck during the Siege of Paris. A melody beginning (read slowly) short E-flat, long A-flat, triplet B-flat, E-flat, B-flat is introduced by a solo trumpet in this opera. The soprano lead of this opera holds a high C before singing (*) "non ti vedro, non ti vedro mai piu" in the aria "O patria mia." A military commander's return is celebrated in a "Grand March" in the second act of this opera, in which the title character is tricked into admitting her love for the commander by Amneris. For 10 points, the Egyptian Radames is the love interest of the title Ethiopian princess in what Giuseppe Verdi opera?

In 1975, an improvised concert at the Cologne Opera House was recorded by a musician who plays this instrument, Keith Jarrett. This instrument was played by the composer of "Honeysuckle Rose" and "Ain't Misbehavin'", Fats Waller. A musician called the "Maharaja" of this instrument recorded Night Train with his band, The (*) Oscar Peterson Trio. A player of this instrument included "Blue Rondo a la Turk" on his album Time Out. "Take Five" and "In a Sentimental Mood" were composed by musicians who played this instrument. For 10 points, Dave Brubeck and Duke Ellington played what keyboard instrument?
2.r: piano [accept pianoforte or electric piano; prompt on keyboard before mention]

2.q: Otto Klemperer disliked the coda of the second movement of this composer's third symphony, and substituted in his own ending for some of his recordings. One symphony by this composer opens with horns playing repeated A-C-sharp dyads before the strings open with an A, C-sharp, A, A, C-sharp, A theme. This composer's fifth symphony quotes the (*) "Dresden Amen" and the hymn "A Mighty Fortress is Our God" This composer's fourth symphony ends with a Saltarello movement that incorporates elements of the tarantella dance, and his third symphony was inspired by travels to a region that also inspired his "Hebrides Overture." For 10 points, name this Jewish composer of the "Scottish" and "Italian" Symphonies.

Astor Piazzolla's The Four Seasons of Buenos Aires is a piece for this many musicians. Franz Schubert's Notturno in E-flat major is a piece for this many performers, as is his late piece The Shepherd on the Rock. Rachmaninoff's piece Romance and Waltz is a piece for this many piano players. A Mozart piece for this many performers is nicknamed Kegelstatt and replaces one of its genre's usual instruments with a clarinet. A Dvorak piece in E minor for this many performers is nicknamed (*) "Dumky." Beethoven's pieces for this many performers include his Opus 1, as well as pieces nicknamed "Ghost" and Archduke." For 10 points, give this number of performers who play in a piano trio.
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt H. Packet 8 Q4

2.q: This composer had a piccolo quote the Andante movement of one of his own symphonies during an aria about a ploughman in spring. Another choral piece by this composer opens in C minor with a loud, held tutti C before a quiet, harmonically ambiguous flattened submediant triad. Later in that piece by this composer, soft pizzicato strings precede a loud, radiant C major chord on the word "Licht," or (*) "Light." Gottfried van Swieten ("SVEE-tin") wrote the libretto for this composer's The Seasons, as well as his oratorio beginning with a "Representation of Chaos" depicting the early universe. A timpani stroke in bar 16 of the second movement accompanies a sudden dynamic change in this composer's Symphony No. 94 in G major, written in London. For 10 points, name this composer of The Creation and the "Surprise" Symphony.

At the finale of one of this composer's works, the chorus warns "Gird on thy sword, thou man of might!" Another of piece his was arranged by Arnold Schoenberg as the Concerto for String Quartet and Orchestra, and another piece in that collection has a larghetto musette as its centerpiece. He's not Corelli, but 12 concerti grossi make up his opus (*) 6. This composer of the funeral anthem "The Ways of Zion do Mourn" included the song "Their Land brought forth frogs" in Israel in Egypt, and also wrote a piece in which Simon sings "Arm, arm ye brave" and the chorus sings "See, the conqu'ring hero comes." For 10 points, name this composer of Judas Maccabaeus who pioneered the English oratorio and included the "Hallelujah" Chorus in his Messiah.

In the orchestral version of Ravel's Tzigane ("tsee-GAHN"), this instrument interrupts the violin's quasi Cadenza at the end of its opening solo. Two of these instruments oscillate between F sharps and G sharps in the opening of Debussy's La Mer, and this instrument is the soloist in Debussy's Sacred and Profane Dances. This instrument joins clarinet, flute, and string quartet in an (*) Introduction and Allegro by Ravel. That piece showcased Erard's double-action version of this instrument. After the opening flute solo of Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, this non-keyboard instrument enters playing a glissando, which can be performed with its 7 pedals or by moving the fingers across its 47 strings. For 10 points, name this large string instrument that is plucked by hand.

This instrument's cadenza over violin tremolos and cymbal ends the violin solo in the orchestral Tzigane ("tsee-GAHN"). Renie ("run-YAY") and Salzedo ("salt-SAY-doh") name methods for playing this instrument. Its special techniques include bisbigliando and pres de la table("pray duh lah TAHB"). It's not the piano, but Pleyel's chromatic version of this instrument was used for Debussy's Sacred and Profane Dances. Its default key is C-flat major. This instrument introduces the "Vysehrad" ("VISH-eh-raht") theme at the beginning of Smetana's Ma vlast. Ravel's (*) Introduction and Allegro features Erard's double-action version of this instrument. This instrument accompanies the violin solos in Scheherazade. A cadenza for it opens the "Waltz of the Flowers" in the Nutcracker. Glissandos for this instrument follow the flute solo at the start of Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. For 10 points, name this instrument with seven pedals and 47 strings that are plucked by hand.

George Enescu called a collection by this composer, which he recorded in both 1940 and 1949, the "Himalayas" of his instrument. A piece by this composer opens with a prelude nearly entirely in sixteenth notes beginning E-D-sharp-E, down to B, G-sharp, B, followed by a movement in the obscure loure ("loo-RAY") dance form. A movement by this composer that Brahms called "a whole world of the deepest thoughts" consists of 64 (*) variations on a four-bar theme. Hilary Hahn's first album includes three of this composer's six Sonatas and Partitas for Solo Violin, one of which ends with a chaconne. Glenn Gould popularized a keyboard piece by this composer consisting of 30 variations on an initial Aria. For 10 points, name this composer of the Goldberg Variations.

The trio of the minuet of Haydn's 96th, or Miracle, symphony features an extended solo for this instrument. In a D major sonata for this instrument, the outer portions of the second movement are marked ad libitum, allowing the performer to determine the tempo; that sonata for this instrument is Saint-Saens's final work. This instrument plays a sad melody at the start of the second movement of Tchaikovsky's fourth symphony. A D minor concerto for this instrument is the best-known work by Baroque composer (*) Alessandro Marcello. It's not the clarinet or viola, but Bach wrote a lot of music for the "d'amore" variant of this instrument. Mozart reworked his C major concerto for this instrument into his second flute concerto. Orchestras tune to the concert A played by this instrument. For 10 points, name this double reed woodwind instrument pitched a fifth higher than the English horn.
2.r: oboes [or hautbois; or French hoboy if you’re a time traveler]

2.q: Two compositions in this genre by Johann Vanhal and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart are nicknamed for publisher Joseph Hoffmeister. Anton Reicha [RAY-khah] composed eight pieces in this genre in Vienna. Ignaz Schuppanzigh premiered many Classical works written for this ensemble. A piece in this genre had its sixth and final movement replaced by an Allegro in B-flat major due to its original ending's (*) dissonant quality. Collections of them by another composer are named "Erdody" [AIR-der-dee] and "Sun." The original finale of the 13th one of these compositions by Beethoven is known as the Grosse Fuge. For 10 points, name these non-symphony compositions pioneered by Joseph Haydn, written for two violins, a viola, and a cello.

One work in this note's major key uses cyclical form and was written for Eugene Ysaye by Cesar Franck, his Violin Sonata. A work in this key by Beethoven has an allegretto second movement with a motif based around a repeating pattern of quarter-eighth-eighth-quarter-quarter, centered on E. This note's major key is the relative major of F-sharp minor, and the key of Beethoven's Kreutzer Sonata and Seventh Symphony. This note's (*) minor key has no accidentals, and is the key of Grieg's Piano Concerto. For 10 points, an orchestra often tunes to the oboe playing this pitch at 440 Hz, the pitch between G-sharp and B-flat.

Pierre Schaeffer's early five "etudes" of this phenomenon gradually led to the formulation of musique concrete. This phenomenon titles a book that opens with a performance of Salome attended by Schoenberg, Puccini, and Mahler. Luigi Russolo built many "intonarumori" machines to espouse his theory outlined in a Futurist manifesto titled for the "art" of this phenomenon. A book by Alex Ross about "Listening to the Twentieth Century" is titled The (*) Rest Is [this word]. A Japanese subgenre of music known by this word includes Pulse Demon by Merzbow. Sonic Youth and The Jesus Lizard are often described as [this word] rock, due to their use of heavy distortion. For 10 points, ambient static is colloquially the "white" type of what unorganized, unpleasant sound?
2.r: noise [accept noise rock; accept Japanoise; accept The Rest Is Noise; accept white noise; accept Cinq études de bruits or Five Studies of Noises; accept The Art of Noises; accept intonarumori or L'arte dei Rumori before mention]

2.q: A short piece by this composer begins with the right hand playing the eighth notes [read slowly] "F A F C F high-F." Several movements of a long piece by this composer include extensive hand-crossing, since they were meant to be played on two keyboards. That piece by this composer includes canons at every interval up to the ninth, as well as a (*) "Quodlibet." This composer included several "little preludes" in a keyboard book for his eldest son, and included songs like "Bist du bei mir" in a Notebook for his second wife. He wrote two books of preludes and fugues in each major and minor key, as well as a piece recorded in 1955 by Glenn Gould. For 10 points, name this composer of the Goldberg Variations and The Well-Tempered Clavier.
2.r: Johann Sebastian Bach [do not accept or prompt on any other Bachs]

2.q: A song composed by this man uses the rising semitones G, G sharp, A, A sharp, B at the end of the bridge, followed by an exact mirror going back into the A section. One of this man's albums depicts cities like Agra, Delhi, and Isfahan that he visited on a world tour. Late in his life, this musician frequently collaborated with the Swedish singer Alice Babs. This composer of "Prelude to a Kiss" had tenor saxophonist Paul Gonsalves play a twenty-seven chorus solo in the middle of his 1956 (*) Newport Jazz Festival rendition of "Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue." The film Black and Tan Fantasy features this man's orchestra, which was the house band of Harlem's Cotton Club, and played a signature tune composed by Billy Strayhorn about a New York subway line. For 10 points, name this jazz bandleader whose orchestra played "Take the 'A' Train," nicknamed the "Duke."

Composer and genre required. In one of these pieces, a descending A-flat major scale ends on E-natural as trumpets and woodwinds enter with fortissimo octave A-flats. The clarinet melody [read slowly] "G, two quick Gs, up to A, G, F-sharp, G, E" opens an E minor one of these pieces. A flute and bassoon duet opens the first of these pieces, titled Winter Dreams. A triplet motif in one of these pieces was described to the composer's patroness Nadezhda von Meck as representing (*) fate. A bass clarinet may be used to play a bassoon solo marked with 6 p's in one of these pieces containing a 5/4 ("five-four") waltz and an Adagio lamentoso fourth movement. The last of these pieces premiered nine days before its composer's death and is nicknamed Pathetique. For 10 points, name these large orchestral pieces by the composer of Swan Lake.
2.r: Tchaikovsky symphonies [or symphonies by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky; accept symphony in place of “symphonies”; prompt on symphony or symphonies by asking “by what composer?”] (The first and fourth lines refer to Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4. The second line refers to Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 5.)

2.q: This composer's first piano concerto originated as a sonata for two pianos, then became a symphony before taking final form. A series of descending thirds in E minor opens a symphony by this composer that was cited by Arnold Schoenberg as an example of why he was a "Progressive." This composer's "F A-flat F" motif referred to him being (*) "free, but happy." Unusually, this 19th-century composer ended his last symphony in E minor with a passacaglia based on a Bach chaconne [shuh-CON]. Hans von Bulow called this composer's first symphony "Beethoven's 10th." For 10 points, name this German composer of four symphonies, the Academic Festival Overture, and a famous Lullaby.

In one movement of this work, the clarinetist plays alternating C and A-flats from offstage to mimic the title effect of being "in the Depths of the Woods." Two keyboardists are instructed to practice scales "awkwardly" in a movement of this work named "The Pianists." The line "It's kind of fun to be extinct" ends one of the (*) Ogden Nash poems written to be read between movements of this work. Ballerina Anna Pavlova's trademark dance is named for a "dying" one of the title creatures from an oft-excerpted cello solo from this suite. Xylophones represent rattling bones in the "Fossils" movement of this work, which is followed by "The Swan." For 10 points, name this zoological suite by Camille Saint-Saens. ("san-sawn").
2.r: The Carnival of the Animals [or Le Carnaval des animaux]

2.q: Producer Orrin Keepnews spliced together 25 different takes to create the title track of one album by a musician of this last name. A composer with this last name known for her braided pigtails called for a soprano and vibrating wineglass in Our Lady of Late, and has the first name Meredith. Songs like "Eronel" and "Misterioso" are part of Milt Jackson's album with the quintet of a musician with this last name. That musician with this last name played celesta on "Pannonica" from his album (*) Brilliant Corners, and also released Genius of Modern Music, which opens with one of the most-recorded jazz standards. For 10 points, "Straight, No Chaser" and "'Round Midnight" are by a jazz pianist with what surname and the first name Thelonious?

This composer's last completed string quartet consists of five Adagio movements and one Adagio molto movement, a funeral march. The motif "G, F-flat, C-flat, B-flat" followed by staccato woodwind chords opens a work by this composer which ends with seven timpani strokes, and which was inspired by another composer's Sinfonia Concertante. This composer wrote two violin concertos in A minor and C-sharp minor for David Oistrakh. Thirteen of this composer's (*) fifteen string quartets were premiered by the Beethoven Quartet. This composer's eighth string quartet features his musical signature (read slowly) D, E-flat, C, B in every movement, and was dedicated "to the victims of fascism and war." For 10 points, name this Russian composer of the Leningrad Symphony.

In the first act of this opera, one character urges "Pursue thy conquest, love!" and "Fear no danger to ensue." This opera ends with cupids being commanded by the chorus "to scatter roses." The penultimate number of this opera is built on a baseline that repeatedly descends chromatically from G to D. In Act 2 of this opera, which includes an "Echo Dance of Furies," a sorceress from a cave summons a "trusted elf" who, disguised as Mercury, commands a character to "stay, (*) Prince." Its third act includes a "Witches' Dance" and a rustic "Sailors' Dance" as the second title character leaves. At the end of this opera, its first title character asks for "Thy Hand, Belinda," and then repeats "Remember me!" in the ground-bass aria "When I am laid in Earth." For 10 points, name this opera by Henry Purcell about a Trojan prince and a queen of Carthage.

A trumpet obsessively quotes the second theme from Chopin's "Funeral March" in a symphony from this country whose second movement has a jazz improvisation between violin and piano. A Mannheim rocket opens another symphony from this country whose main theme is played first in D major, then repeated in C major. Benjamin Britten dedicated his Cello Symphony and cello sonata to a cellist from this country, and (*) Van Cliburn won a 1958 piano competition in this country by performing works by two of its composers. Alfred Schnittke was from this country, as was a composer whose first symphony was nicknamed "Classical". One composer from this country wrote his fifth symphony in response to the editorial "Muddle Instead of Music", and included an "invasion theme" in his seventh. For 10 points, name this home of Sergei Prokofiev and Dmitri Shostakovich.
2.r: The Soviet Union [or Russia; or Union of Soviet Socialist Republics; or USSR; or SSSR; or CCCP]

2.q: A theme from a piece in this collection was borrowed from a sinfonia in Il Giustino. In another work from this collection, the first violin comes in on measure 4 playing repeated eight-note B-flat trills while the rest of the strings play repeated eighth notes. The first of these pieces begins with (read slowly) "E, G-sharp, G-sharp, G-sharp, F-sharp, E, B." One section of that piece depicts a (*) sleeping goatherd. The viola section represents a barking dog in one of these works. This group of violin concertos was published in a larger set called The Contest Between Harmony and Invention. For 10 points, name these Antonio Vivaldi works that include "Winter" and "Spring."
2.r: The Four Seasons [or Le quatro stagioni; prompt on Vivaldi violin concertos; prompt on The Contest Between Harmony and Invention before mention; prompt on Spring or Winter before mention]

2.q: In a sad, slow movement of this piece, muted strings repeat the rising theme [read slowly] "F-sharp, B, long C-sharp," steadily building up to a climax then fading out. A triangle roll and a held note on muted upper strings introduce a triple-time dance in this piece marked "Tempo di mazurka." A solo flute opens a movement in this piece by descending in E major pentatonic from B to E, then rising back up to B. Another movement of this piece is built around a theme of six mostly rising (*) staccato eighth notes followed by a quarter note, which is traded by the bassoons and low strings. This piece contains "Anitra's Dance" and "Ase's Death," as well as a movement in B minor that grows to a loud climax as it depicts gnomes, goblins, and trolls singing in the title location. For 10 points, "In the Hall of the Mountain King" is part of what suite by Edvard Grieg?
2.r: Peer Gynt [or Peer Gynt Suites; accept any section of the incidental music to Peer Gynt, such as “Åse’s Death” or “Anitra’s Dance”]

2.q: Elliott Carter's double concerto is scored for two chamber orchestras, piano and this instrument, and the role for that instrument was premiered by Ralph Kirkpatrick. "Les baricades misterieuses" was composed for this instrument, and the composer of that work wrote 4 books of solo works for this instrument which are themselves divided into 27 "orders"; those books are by (*) Francois Couperin. Baldassare Galuppi learned to play it from organist Antonio Lotti and composed numerous concerti for it. Poulenc's Concert champetre was composed for Wanda Landowska, a 20th century master of it. Like the muselar and virginal, this instrument produces sound by plucking strings with picks attached to keys. For 10 points, name this keyboard instrument popular in the Baroque era.

Bela Bartok's variation on this technique is indicated using a circle with a vertical line intersecting it at 12 o'clock. This technique is used throughout the third movement of Tchaikovsky's Symphony No. 4 and the second movement of Ravel's String Quartet in F. A plus symbol indicates the one-handed version of this technique in the last of a set of caprices by (*) Paganini. After passages employing this technique, the term arco is used to return to normal playing. The name for this technique is Italian for "pinched." For 10 points, what musical technique involves plucking the strings instead of bowing them?

A 20th-century concerto for this instrument opens with the cellos playing soft "D-E-D-E" twice in a thematic fragment that repeats throughout the piece. A "Romance" and "Humoresque" are the two movements of Carl Nielsen's two Fantasy Pieces for this instrument and piano. The American soldier John de Lancie inspired a late concerto for this instrument based on the short-short-short-long motif, written by (*) Richard Strauss. In the first movement of Beethoven's fifth symphony, a brief cadenza for this instrument leads into the recapitulation. In Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf, this instrument represents the duck. For 10 points, the English horn is the lower "cousin" of what double reed instrument that the orchestra tunes to?

This piece opens with four cellos and two violins playing the hymn "O Lord, Save Thy People." A brass fanfare alternating with chaotically struck tubular bells gives way to descending strings that lead into the final section of this piece. This piece debuted in 1882 at the Cathedral of Christ the Savior, a building dedicated to the event this piece commemorates. The Battle of (*) Borodino is represented in this piece by the increasing prominence of "La Marseillaise." ("mar-say-yez")." The melody of "God Save the Tsar!" appears in the grand finale of this piece, which calls for several live cannon shots. For 10 points, identify this overture by Tchaikovsky, named for the year Napoleon retreated from Russia.

As a sixteen-year old, this musician once played so badly that drummer Jo Jones threw a cymbal at him. Due to a contract dispute, this musician played in Toronto under the alias "Charlie Chan" and used a plastic Grafton saxophone on the album Jazz at Massey Hall. A modified 12-bar blues progression is named for this musician's standard (*) "Blues for Alice". Dizzy Gillespie played piano instead of trumpet on a recording of this musician's pioneering bebop standard "Ko-Ko" and Gillespie also composed "Anthropology" with this musician. For 10 points, the standard "Ornithology" was composed by what saxophonist nicknamed "Bird"?

In an essay by John Darnielle, this composer inspires the singer to think of "U.G. Krishnamurti...Current 93...and endless smoke". After a dialogue with Toru Takemitsu, this composer decided to translate a Basho haiku as "What mushroom? / What leaf?" With the violinist Paul Zukofsky, this man composed the Freeman Etudes. The St. Burchadi Church in Halberstadt is the site of this composer's very long organ piece As Slow as Possible. Performances of a 1951 indeterminate composition by this composer are guided by the (*) I Ching. David Tudor premiered this composer's piece Music of Changes. This composer of the Imaginary Landscapes series made early, and regular, use of the prepared piano. For 10 points, name this minimalist composer of 4'33".

This composer's Opus 16 includes the pieces "Premonitions" and "Peripeteia." This composer's song sets include his Four Orchestral Songs, Opus 22, and the cycle Book of the Hanging Gardens. This composer discussed the "musical prose" of "Brahms, the Progressive" in an essay from Style and Idea. He coined the term "developing variation," and he described melody generated from changing timbres in his book Harmonielehre. His Opus 9 is notated in E major and called (*) Chamber Symphony No. 1. This composer of Gurre-Lieder used piano, violin, cello, flute, and clarinet to accompany twenty-one songs using a hybrid singing-speaking technique. This composer wrote of the "emancipation of the dissonance," pioneered atonality in works like Verlkarte Nacht ("fuh-CLARE-tuh NOKHT"), and created the twelve-tone system. For 10 points, name this Second Viennese School composer of Pierrot Lunaire.

This bandleader remixed the Scritti Politti song "Perfect Way" on the first of his collaboration albums with Marcus Miller, which was criticized for its use of synthesizers and drum machines. That album, Tutu, followed up on an album by this musician that was finally released in September 2019, titled Rubberband. A third album by this jazz artist begins with a chord held on the organ by Joe Zawinul ("ZAH-vih-null") on the track "Shhh/Peaceful." (*) Wayne Shorter stayed on from this musician's Second Great Quintet to work on that first fusion album by this musician, titled In A Silent Way. Earlier, this bandleader worked with arranger Gil Evans on an album that included "Freddie Freeloader" and "So What." For 10 points, name this bandleader and trumpeter on the album Kind of Blue.

In an early piece, this composer used the Phrygian mode for an antiphon to the Virgin Mary, Salve intemerata. This composer included "Magnificat" and "Nunc dimittis" sections in his Short Service in the Dorian Mode. A contemporary ensemble named for this composer's "Scholars" helped to repopularize early a capella vocal music. A work by this composer that ends "respice humilitatem nostram" is scored for eight (*) choirs of five voices and was written for a monarch's fortieth birthday. A later composer's orchestral work reuses a Phrygian melody that this composer wrote in honor of Archbishop Parker, "Why fum'th in fight." This composer and his student, William Byrd, were given a monopoly on publishing polyphonic music by Elizabeth I. For 10 points, name this English Renaissance composer who wrote Spem in alium and inspired a Fantasia by Ralph (rafe) Vaughan (von) Williams.

The timpani plays beats under a C-minor violin theme in 6/8 time in the un poco sostenuto first movement of a symphony by this composer. The final movement of that symphony features a horn solo containing an alphorn-inspired theme. This composer composed two clarinet sonatas and a Clarinet Quintet in B minor for Richard (*) Muhlfeld. The Bach cantata Nach dir, Herr, verlanget mich was the basis for a passacaglia that ends this composer's fourth and final symphony. This composer responded "any ass can see that" to an assertion that his first symphony quoted "Ode to Joy." Hans von Bulow dubbed this composer's first symphony "Beethoven's tenth." For 10 points, name this German composer of four symphonies and a famous lullaby.

One of this opera's leitmotifs consists of the short-long descending fourths C G, then F C, then the tritone A D-sharp. At the beginning of this opera, a girl promises to throw a tiny green flower to the man who takes her to the cistern. That girl praises another man whose body "was like an ivory column." It later features a quintet of arguing Jews, and ends with the instruction, "kill the woman!" A dissonant chord played sforzando near the end of this work has been called "the most (*) sickening chord in all opera." That chord is played just after the title soprano says, "I have now kissed thy mouth," to the severed head of Jochanaan. A body double is sometimes used when that soprano gains the favor of her stepfather, Herod, by performing the Dance of the Seven Veils. For 10 points, name this opera with a libretto based on a play by Oscar Wilde with music by Richard Strauss.
2.c: 2015 STIMPY Pkt 01. Chicago A - MIT B Q19

2.q: Charles Villiers Stanford wrote a set of six rhapsodies named for this country. Though he is not from this country, a composer whose surname is the same as this country wrote the motet "Greater Love Has No Man" and the hymn "The Holy Boy." A composer from this country is credited with writing the first nocturnes. The cruit (crit) and the clairseach (CLOOR-sha) are harp-like instruments used in this country's traditional folk music. (*) Riverdance is a theatrical show featuring the traditional music of this country. Traditional ballads originating in this country include Molly Malone and Danny Boy. For 10 points, name this country of origin of John Field, whose traditional music often utilizes the fiddle to play jigs.
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt J. Packet 10 Q5

2.q: This composer's first symphony, which he submitted and resubmitted for criticism to his teacher Nikolai Zaremba, nearly led to his mental breakdown. This man used his material from his unpublished opera Undine in the second movement of his C-minor second symphony, whose basis in Ukrainian folk songs led to a nickname coined by Nikolai Kashkin. This composer's final symphony, which contains a (*) "limping waltz" in 5/4 time, was premiered just nine days before his death and dedicated to his homosexual lover. For 10 points, name this composer of the symphonies nicknamed Little Russian, Winter Daydreams, and Pathetique, who also composed the "1812 Overture."
2.c: 2013 Minnesota Undergraduate Tournament (MUT) Pkt EPacket 5 Proofread Q5

2.q: Nikolai Kapustin wrote a set of 24 of these pieces "in jazz style." A collection of these pieces dedicated to Joseph Kessler includes one beginning descending "F, short D-flat, A-flat" in the right hand. A Bach work of this type was the inspiration for Gounod's "Ave Maria." Frederic Chopin's Opus 28 No. 15 is a piece of this type evoking the title phenomenon with a repeating (*) A-flat in the left hand. That work, "Raindrop," belongs to a collection of these pieces in all 24 major and minor keys, which mirrors an earlier Baroque composer's collection. For 10 points, name these introduction pieces paired with fugues in J. S. Bach's The Well-Tempered Clavier.

In the first movement coda of a symphony by this composer, the brass twice play a Neapolitan E-flat major chord over a D pedal point. The most popular completion of that unfinished symphony is by Samale and Mazzuca, though the composer suggested using his Te Deum as a finale. A symphony by this composer begins with a horn playing B-flat, E-flat, B-flat, then C-flat, E-flat, B-flat over tremolo strings. That symphony's scherzo has enigmatic markings like "Jagdthema" and "Volksfest". Deryck Cooke gave this man's name to the (*) problem of sifting through the many versions of his symphonies. A cymbal clash and a quartet of Wagner tubas figure in this composer's seventh symphony. Many of his symphonies have motifs of two quarter-notes followed by a quarter-note triplet, this man's namesake rhythm. For 10 points, name this Austrian acolyte of Wagner who wrote the "Lyric" and "Romantic" symphonies.

This composer's "On Parade" is one of the few "screamers" he composed. Vladimir Horowitz made a 1945 virtuosic piano transcription of a piece by this composer. The flowing (read slowly) "E-flat, E-flat, D-flat, C, C, B-natural, C, C" begins the main theme of a piece by this composer. That piece contains a (*) piccolo obbligato that represents the South. Works by this composer include "Hands Across the Sea" and "The Liberty Bell," and an instrument named for this composer often replaces the tuba in marching bands. For 10 points, name this American "March King" who composed "The Stars and Stripes Forever."

This composer's third symphony begins with the cellos and basses playing a brisk theme that begins with four repeated Cs, then descends down the major scale to G. He's not William Walton, but this composer's third symphony premiered along with his incidental music to Belshazzar's Feast. The third movement of this composer's second symphony leads attacca into its D-major triumphant finale. Horns mimic (*) swan calls in the third movement of a symphony by this composer. This composer's one-movement seventh symphony in C major was his last before a thirty year "silence." A patriotic tone poem by this composer had to be performed under alternative titles to avoid Russian censorship. For 10 points, name this composer of Finlandia.

In the first movement of a symphony by this composer, stacked fourths over a repeated rhythm of a dotted eighth note and two thirty-second notes lead into the E minor primary theme. In this composer's last finished symphony, a trumpet solo interrupts a dissonant Rondo-Burleske with a lyrical melody that recurs in the finale, which is in D flat and ends with the marking "dying away." This composer of a work nicknamed (*) "Song of the Night," which includes parts for mandolin and tenor horn, began his six-movement third symphony with eight unison horns playing a Brahms-inspired melody. The third movement of that work by this composer is interrupted by a posthorn, while its fourth movement includes an alto solo that quotes from Nietzsche's Also Sprach Zarathustra. For 10 points, name this late Romantic composer, whose other symphonies include those titled "Titan" and "Resurrection."

One player of this instrument composed a cantata cycle in which each movement is dedicated to a different part of Christ's body. The "Orpheus of Amsterdam", Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck ("YAN PEE-tuh-zoon SVAY-link"), played this instrument. Concertos for this instrument were developed by Handel as interludes between the acts of his oratorios. In the seventeenth century, this instrument had a North (*) German and South German school of performance, the former of which included Dieterich Buxtehude ("BUX-tuh-hoo-duh"). A mordent on A followed by a descent down to C-sharp begins a piece for this instrument usually attributed to J. S. Bach, who also wrote a G minor "Little" fugue for it. Players of this instrument pull out stops to alter its sound. For 10 points, name this keyboard instrument that creates sound by pushing air through pipes and is often found in churches.
2.r: organ [or pipe organ] (The cantata cycle is Membra Jesu Nostri by Buxtehude.)

2.q: A piano intermezzo by Arnold Bax is titled this word "in exile." This thing titles Scriabin's secretly-written first orchestral piece. La Monte Young named both a chord with a fourth, tritone, and fifth and a "House" of endless sound in New York after this word. In a piano piece titled for this thing, the 6th iteration of a rising C, long F, E F A C motif resolves to G major 9. Poems about kinds of love inspired three Liszt nocturnes also titled for this thing; the third one opens with a melody under A-flat major arpeggios. After killing his beloved in this state, the (*) obsessed artist is depicted by a two-octave falling C minor scale and syncopated march to the scaffold before a witches' sabbath in Symphonie fantastique. This state titles the calm 7th movement of Schumann's Kinderszenen ("kin-dust-SAY-nin"), Traumerei ("TROY-muh-rye"). For 10 points, what word is at the end of the title of Mendelssohn's incidental music for a Shakespeare play?
2.r: dream [or daydream, rêve, rêverie, songe, or Träume; accept dream chord or Dream House; accept Liebesträume or Dreams of Love; accept Träumerei until read; accept Midsummer Night’s Dream; do not accept “drugged”]

2.q: In a song by this group, a choir repeats the verse "hold on; if love is the answer, you're home." This group collaborated with Leiji ("lay-jee") Matsumoto on Interstella 5555, an animated film featuring a blue-skinned pop band. This group's song "Touch" features in a video where a member of this group removes their leather jacket to reveal a switch on their back that activates a (*) self-destruct countdown. This group was sampled in Kanye West's song "Stronger." In a song by this group, Pharrell Williams sings that "we've come too far to give up who we are." For 10 points, name this French dance music group behind the songs "Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger" and "Get Lucky," whose members wore robot helmets.

A popular genre influenced by this ethnic group's percussion heavily features the sekere ("SHEH-keh-reh") rattle, and later the pedal steel guitar on albums like Synchro System. Performers called ayan from this ethnic group play the dundun ("doon-doon"), its version of the talking drum. A saxophonist from this ethnic group quoted one of its proverbs about nature's indispensability on the 1975 track "Water No Get Enemy." The albums Expensive Shit and (*) Zombie are by a musician from this ethnic group. Musicians from this ethnic group include the juju musician King Sunny Ade, as well as Afrobeat founder Fela Kuti. This ethnic group's complex bata drumming can be heard in Santeria ceremonies in Cuba, whose veneration of orishas derives from this ethnic group. For 10 points, name this ethnic group, the largest in Nigeria along with the Hausa and Igbo.

A Tigran Mansurian piece in this genre is dedicated to victims of the Armenian Genocide and uses elements of Armenian folk music in its composition. Organ and trombone dominate the Tuba mirum movement of Saint-Saens' piece in this genre. Giuseppe Verdi's best known non-opera piece is his piece in this genre composed in honor of Alessandro Manzoni. Wilfred Owen poems were used as part of the text to a piece of this genre by Benjamin Britten, named for (*) "War." Franz Sussmayr completed a piece in this genre in D minor after the death of its primary composer in 1791. These pieces usually contain movements like Agnus Dei and Dies Irae. Faure and Mozart both composed notable examples of, for 10 points, what pieces often called "Masses for the Dead?"
2.r: Requiem Mass [accept Mass for the Dead until mentioned; prompt on mass]
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt K. Packet 11 Q18

2.q: A "Hymn to the Wilderness" opens an opera by this composer that ends with a plot to reach the title Invisible City. In an opera by this composer, the title character chooses the third sister as his bride to the dismay of the old woman Babarikha [ba-ba-REEK-uh]. A seven-scene opera by this composer is partly set in the realm of the Sea-King and includes three arias depicting the Varangian, Indian, and Venetian guest. The "Procession of the (*) Nobles" is played while the title princess returns as a spirit in this composer's opera Mlada. Rapid descending chromatic notes open a frantic passage from an opera by this composer of Sadko that occurs after the Swan-Bird changes Prince Gvidon Saltanovich into an insect. For 10 points, name this Russian composer whose opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan includes the "Flight of the Bumblebee."

This composer wrote a four-movement piece that contains a first movement Andante tranquillo fugue and a third-movement with timpani glissandi and a xylophone solo based on the Fibonacci sequence. A one-act pantomime ballet by this composer includes three "seduction games," after which the title character chases the girl. This man, who pioneered a dissonance-rich style known as (*) "night music," wrote a piece that includes the movements "Intermezzo interrotto" and "Game of Pairs." This composer wrote The Miraculous Mandarin and Music for Strings, Percussion, and Celesta. For 10 points, name this man who wrote the Concerto for Orchestra, a twentieth-century composer from Hungary.
2.c: 2013 Minnesota Undergraduate Tournament (MUT) Pkt KPacket 11 Proofread Q8

2.q: A country singer with this first name hopes that her ex-lover has got "movin' on all figured out, and you don't hate me somehow" in a duet with Lee Brice titled "I Hope You're Happy Now". In a 1972 song, an artist with this first name described a man who "probably think(s) this song is about you". A singer with this first name states "I'll be your sinner in secret" and exhorts the addressee to (*) "Run Away with Me" in a song from her 2015 album Emotion. That singer claims "before you came into my life, I missed you so bad" in a hit where she states "I just met you and this is crazy". For 10 points, give this first name of the singer of "Call Me Maybe".
2.r: Carly [accept Carly Pearce or Carly Cristyne Slusser; accept Carly Simon; accept Carly Rae Jepsen]

2.q: Composer and type of piece required. A polka in the ninth of these non-symphonic pieces includes a C-sharp ostinato inspired by the galop from William Tell. The first of these pieces to be written as a five-movement cycle features subtitles such as "Calm unawareness of the future cataclysm" that evoke a war story. A scherzo in one of these pieces was likely intended as a suicide note retrospective with quotes of pieces such as its composer's E-flat major (*) cello concerto. An ensemble named for Alexander Borodin previewed these pieces for its composer, including one written while he was scoring the film Five Days, Five Nights in Dresden. That piece dedicated "to the victims of Fascism and War" opens with somber statements of the cryptomotif "D, E-flat, C, B."For 10 points, name these pieces by the composer of the Leningrad Symphony for two violins, viola, and cello.
2.r: string quartets by Dmitri Shostakovich [prompt on partial answer] (The quartets clued are Shostakovich’s ninth, third, and eighth quartets, respectively; the Borodin quartet previewed the quartets for Shostakovich before they were premiered, while the Beethoven Quartet usually premiered them.)

2.q: Composer and type of piece required. A passage from one of these pieces begins with a high D, before a series of rising left-hand octave arpeggios rooted on the following (read slowly) -- "B, C, A, B, G, A, F-sharp, G" -- mirrored by falling right-hand arpeggios. That one of these pieces, transcribed for two players by Edvard Grieg, oddly recapitulates its first movement's theme in the subdominant, F major. One of these in the key of A begins with a triple-time Andante grazioso on the notes (read slowly) "dotted C-sharp, D, C-sharp, then two long Es". Heavy (*) Alberti bass accompanies the right hand's (read slowly) "C, E, G, B, C-D-C" at the opening of a C major example of these pieces known as facile ("FAH-chee-lay") or "Simple". The eleventh of these pieces closes by evoking Ottoman bands in its Rondo alla turca. For 10 points, name these pieces for solo keyboard by an Austrian child prodigy.
2.r: piano sonatas by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart [prompt on piano sonatas or sonatas ; prompt on Mozart piano pieces or Mozart sonatas]

2.q: This artist's debut album was released after her record label TDE took her hard drive in 2017. This artist sang "I get so lonely, I forget what I'm worth" on a song inspired by the star of the film Poison Ivy. This artist described "feeling like Jericho" and a "new bitch on my nerves" in two songs from her 2022 album, whose Princess Diana-inspired cover shows her sitting on a (*) diving board. This artist declared "his new girlfriend's next" and "I'd rather be in jail than alone" in a song named after a Quentin Tarantino film. For 10 points, name this R&B artist of "Good Days" and "Shirt" who declared "I might kill my ex" in "Kill Bill".

A recitative from this opera references its first aria by beginning with the notes C-C-B in C minor. A thunderclap concludes an "echo dance" from the "witches scene" of this opera's second act. A strangely joyful sea shanty about taking a "boozy short leave" opens this opera's third act. Two dances in the early score for this opera suggest its composer called for guitar in the continuo. A repeated chromatic descent from G to D serves as the textbook example of ground (*) bass in this opera's final aria. This opera, with libretto by Nahum Tate, was inspired by John Blow's Venus and Adonis. This opera's protagonist sings "Thy hand, Belinda" right before "When I am Laid in Earth," her so-called "Lament." For 10 points, name this baroque opera by Henry Purcell about the Queen of Carthage and a Trojan prince.

Recordings of an early modern genre of music invented by this religious denomination, the choral concerto, have been released by the PaTRAM Institute. Simple diatonic ornamentation is used in a 2-part form of chant from this denomination called Valaam. An orchestral piece based on this denomination's music opens with woodwinds playing (read slowly) "F, F, F, E, D" in a 5/2 ("five-two") time rhythm. Another orchestral piece opens with two violas and four cellos playing a (*) hymn from this denomination, "Lord Save Thy People," which begins "E-flat, E-flat, F, G" and is an example of a troparion. A book of chants from this denomination, the Obikhod ("OH-bee-khod"), provided the music for an "Easter Festival Overture". For 10 points, what denomination's music inspired much work by the Mighty Five, including Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov?
2.r: Russian Orthodox Church [or Eastern Orthodox Church; prompt on Orthodox or Orthodoxy; prompt on Russian Church]

2.q: A collection of these pieces uses six different kinds of opening movements, last movements in six different time signatures, and six different keys: B-flat major, C minor, A minor, D major, G major, and E minor. It doesn't refer to a specific ensemble, but the sonata da camera followed the same format as this genre. The "standard" format of these pieces was established by Froberger. One of eight of these pieces Handel published in 1720 ends with "The Harmonious Blacksmith." A B-minor piece in this genre was paired with the (*) Italian Concerto in the second volume of Bach's Clavier-Ubung. In Germany, these pieces were often named for beginning with a French Overture. Other names for this genre include "ordre" and "partita." They typically include a gigue, a sarabande, a courante, and an allemande. French harpsichord composers like Rameau and Couperin bundled their pieces as works in this genre. Bach wrote "French" and "English" collections of these pieces. For 10 points, name this genre of six Bach pieces for solo cello.
2.r: suites [accept French overture, ordre, or partitauntil those words are read; accept more specific answers like cello suites]

2.q: Thomas Ades drew upon the Book of Genesis for his first work in this genre, In Seven Days. Khachaturian used a musical saw in the second movement of his D-flat major piece in this genre. The orchestra gradually joins the double basses and a solo contrabassoon in the opening of a piece in this genre that features a dramatic cadenza starting on an A in octaves. A work in this genre begins with tense, whole-note chords that crescendo from pianissimo as the (*) soloist plays low F's. A jazzy, Basque-influenced G major work in this genre begins with a whip-crack. Yannick Nezet-Seguin conducted a 2023 "marathon" of four of these pieces with soloist Yuja Wang. Paul Wittgenstein commissioned Ravel to write a work in this genre for the left hand. For 10 points, name this type of piece for orchestra and a solo keyboard instrument.

Hector Berlioz failed to win the Prix de Rome with a cantata titled for the death of this figure that is subtitled "Monologue et Bacchanale." Christoph Willibald Gluck's opera about this character includes a "Dance of the Furies" followed by "The Dance of the Blessed Spirits" as the title character moves into the Elysian Fields. A can-can is accompanied by an (*) "infernal gallop" in an opera about this mythological figure "in the Underworld." For 10 points, the first true opera is considered to be what work by Claudio Monteverdi titled for the mythological musician married to Eurydice?

In his last concert, Leonard Bernstein led this city's orchestra in a performance of Beethoven's 7th symphony. In 2018, this city's orchestra allied with the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra, since they are both directed by the Latvian-born Andris Nelsons. This city's orchestra premiered Bartok's Concerto for Orchestra, which was commissioned by its director Serge Koussevitzky, who names a concert hall at that orchestra's summer home in (*) Tanglewood. This city is home to the easternmost of the "Big Five" American orchestras. John Williams is the Laureate Conductor of a subset of this city's orchestra that focuses on light music and is known for its 4th of July concerts. For 10 points, Arthur Fiedler led a namesake "Pops" Orchestra in what capital of Massachusetts?

The most famous movement from these works begins with a long, sustained F-sharp in the violins over a walking bass that slowly goes down the scale from D to G. The first of these works is in C major, includes a Forlana, and concludes with a Passepied. The third and fourth of these works are both in D major and include three trumpets and timpani. The second one of these works is in B minor, features a solo flute, and ends with a (*) Badinerie. Only the third of them ends with a Gigue, but all four of these works begin with French overtures. The second movement of the third one of these works has become known as "Air on the G String." For 10 points, name these four sets of dances for large ensemble by J. S. Bach.
2.r: Bach’s Orchestral Suites [or Ouvertures; accept reasonable equivalents like Suites for Orchestra; prompt on “suites”]

2.q: The "Pavana Lachrymae" movement of George Crumb's Black Angels quotes a piece by this composer. Ferdinand Troyer commissioned this composer's Octet in F, scored for string quartet, horn, basson, clarinet and double bass. This composer adapted one of his songs into his 14th string quartet, written during the same period of sickness that produced his (*) Rosamunde quartet. This composer again drew on his earlier lied "Die Forelle" for a five-performer chamber work featuring a double bass and piano. Death and the Maiden and The Trout Quintet are chamber works by this composer whose cycles of lieder include Winterreise and Die Schоne Mullerin. For 10 points, what German composer left his eighth symphony in B minor unfinished at his death?
2.c: 2019 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt F. Packet 6 Q24

2.q: A composer from this country who developed a namesake method for teaching children music that includes using hand signs wrote the opera Hary Janos [HA-ree YA-nosh]. Brahms composed a set of 21 dances based on the czardas [chahr-dahsh] from this country. Another composer from this country wrote the ballet The Miraculous Mandarin and an opera in which Judith discovers that her husband's dead wives are hidden behind a forbidden door. That composer of (*) Duke Bluebeard's Castle is Bela Bartok, who was born in this country. For 10 points, Franz Liszt [list] wrote a set of rhapsodies named for what central European country?

A cantata by a composer with this first name with the subtitle "lyric humoresque" is set during springtime on their home island. The third symphony of a composer with this first name opens with twenty-six unison A's from the orchestra, and calls for wordless baritone and soprano parts. Another composer with this first name used three glockenspiels to open the movement "Blanziflor et Helena," part of the first entry in his musical triptych (*) Trionfi. A cantata by a composer with this first name that unusually opens in 3/1 time includes the section "In the Tavern," which features a falsetto tenor aria depicting the roasting of a swan. That composer with this first name set Goliardic poems in a cantata beginning with the entry "O Fortuna." For 10 points, give this first name of the composer of Carmina Burana, surnamed Orff.

A type of music described by this noun is exemplified by two concerto movements marked adagio religioso, and the third movement Elegia from a work that also contains a fourth-movement "Intermezzo Interrotto". The second and fourth movements of Mahler's 7th symphony are explicitly titled for this noun. A G major serenade for strings with this noun in its usual English translation has a second movement C major Romanze and opens with a Mannheim Rocket. A character titled for this (*) time period sings one of her two arias immediately following the tenor aria "" and her other aria requires her to sing a high F6. That character named for this time period attempts to convince Tamino to rescue her daughter Pamina. For 10 points, a Queen named for which time period appears in The Magic Flute?

This composer used a plagal half-cadence to end the exposition of one piece's first movement. Schoenberg orchestrated this man's Piano Quartet No. 1 and wrote an essay about this man "the Progressive." This composer used a natural horn in his Horn Trio and wrote his Clarinet Trio and Clarinet Quintet for Richard Muhlfeld. He used the likely misattributed "Chorale St. Antoni" as the basis for his Variations on a Theme of (*) Haydn. Another of his works is based around a motif first presented as F-A-B flat and sets texts from the Luther Bible. This composer quoted from student songs like "Fuchslied" and "Gaudeamus igitur" in a piece often paired with the Tragic Overture. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer of Academic Festival Overture, the Hungarian Dances, and A German Requiem.

A musician who primarily played this instrument developed a tune he nervously whistled while waiting for his first plane ride into the song "Flying Home." Tal Farlow and Charles Mingus joined the "trio" of a bandleader who played this instrument, Red Norvo. One player of this instrument referenced the nickname he got for being perpetually sleepless in the title of his standard "Bags' Groove." Milt Jackson, a member of the Modern Jazz Quartet, played this instrument, as did (*) Lionel Hampton. Gary Burton promoted the "four-mallet" style of playing this instrument as an alternative to the "two-mallet" style. This instrument has a bunch of fans that can rapidly open and close the tubular resonators underneath, creating an undulating pitch. For 10 points, name this percussion instrument with tuned metal bars, named for its ability to pulsate.

At the end of one symphony's lento third movement, this composer wrote an attacca that is often interrupted by an excerpt from The Sun Rising. In one symphony, this composer drew from an H.G. Wells quote about a "passing river" for an epilogue following the motif "C, E, D, long G, C, D, E, long C." The line "I do not regret this journey" is recited in a symphony by this composer whose "Landscape" third movement uses a (*) wind machine. A brass fanfare in a symphony by this composer is answered by a chorus singing, "Behold [the title entity]," in a setting of Walt Whitman. A solo harp mimics the Westminster chimes in this composer's "London" symphony, written in the same year as a piece with a violin cadenza depicting the title bird of a George Meredith poem. For 10 points, name this British composer of A Sea Symphony and The Lark Ascending.
2.r: Ralph Vaughan Williams (The H.G. Wells quote is from “Night and the Open Sea” in Tono-Bungay.)

2.q: Jane Fulcher's book The Nation as Art rejects the traditional thesis that this style rose in prominence due to the influence of Louis Veron. In a composition in this style, deceased women rise from their tombs to seduce a knight in the "Ballet of the Nuns." The prayer "Nume del Ciel" ("NOO-may del CHELL") is sung before battle in another composition in this style that ends with an eruption of Mount Vesuvius. In a third composition in this style, the ringing of a bell signals the beginning of a (*) massacre, after which Raoul jumps out a window. Canonically, the earliest work in this style is Daniel Auber's ("don-YELL oh-BAY's") The Mute Girl of Portici. Works in this style include Hector Berlioz's Les Troyens ("lay twah-YANN") and most of the output of Giacomo Meyerbeer ("JAH-ko-mo MY-er-beer"). For 10 points, name this dominant style of opera in early 19th-century France characterized by lavish designs and very large orchestras.
2.r: grand operas [or grand opéra (“GRON top-pay-RAH”); prompt on operas; prompt on Romantic opera/style; prompt on French opera or Paris opera]

3.q: Keith Emerson's thirteen-year-old grandson Ethan recorded Keith's The Dreamer with this orchestra on a 2018 tribute album conducted by Terje Mikkelsen. With this orchestra, Anthony Marwood recorded the violin concerto of Sally Beamish, who in 2018 was named this orchestra's first composer in residence. Its second music director conducted the orchestra from the violin section, until rheumatoid arthritis in her wrists forced her to stop playing in 1998. (*) Iona Brown directed this orchestra, for which Christopher Hogwood played continuo, before he left due to its practice of performing early music on modern instruments. This orchestra recorded popular Mozart selections for the film Amadeus under its founder, Neville Marriner, who named it after the London church in which it performed. For 10 points, name this chamber orchestra that, despite its name, is not a school in the countryside.
3.r: The Academy of St.-Martin-in-the-Fields [or the ASMF; prompt on St.-Martin-in-the-Fields]

3.q: One composer from this country used a Brahms-inspired Lamento motif in his horn trio, meant to represent a third way that was neither modern or postmodern. That composer from this country used two string ensembles tuned a quarter note apart in his Ramifications. Another composer from this country was a noted proponent of an ABCBA "arch form" which lent symmetry to his 4th and 5th string quartets. (*) Micropolyphony and night music were two styles employed by composers from this country. The latter of those composers names a type of forceful pizzicato and wrote Music for Percussion, Strings and Celesta. For 10 points, name this country home to Gyorgi Ligeti and Bela Bartok.
3.c: 2017 Oxford Open Pkt 03 - Ostentatious Hydromancy Q15

3.q: A C-sharp minor piece by this composer symbolises the cross in its opening motif, according to musicologist John Butt. This composer used unusual combinations of signatures, such as E-flat minor and 3/2 time, or G major and 24/16 time, in a piece that inspired both the Op. 87 of Dmitri Shostakovich and a B minor arrangement by Alexander Siloti. He did not work in England, but this composer often signed his pieces with the abbreviations "J.N.J." or "S.D.G." Hans von Bulow ("BYOO-loh") contrasted one of this composer's pieces with Beethoven's piano sonatas, which he called the (*) "New Testament."
